newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders call for treaty talks to move apace.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders call for treaty talks to move apace.

text.p: European Union leaders, seeking to reinvigorate talks on the bloc's future, pledged again on Saturday to complete a new treaty by the middle of next year and rejected any idea of scaling back its scope.
"Like cyclists going up a hill, we have decided to get out of the saddle and push harder," Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said.

At a special summit called to discuss talks on a new EU treaty, leaders expressed concern that without progress on reforming the bloc their plans to accept new countries from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean would be disrupted.
"If there is a failure...this will be carried over to enlargement," French President Jacques Chirac told reporters. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said delay in the talks would be "very dangerous".
The leaders reaffirmed that they want the talks -- the inter-governmental conference (IGC) -- to end at the Amsterdam summit set for June 1997 and to produce substantial results.
"At the end of the day, governments are going to have to cut a deal to get a treaty. That is going to happen now in June 1997," said Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, host of the summit.
Chirac and Kohl both said there had been substantial support among the leaders to reinforce joint foreign policy decision- making among the bloc's members.
They had also held a long discussion about crime and the fight against drugs.

Leaders were at pains to deny they were scaling down their ambitions, after speculation prompted by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's comments that more reforms would be needed to EU institutions even after the current treaty talks.

Kohl said reports that this meant he wanted a postponement of the IGC were "absurd". He said he had meant that five or 10 years after the new treaty was approved there might be a need for more revisions.

But the prospect of British general elections next May has prompted speculation that a hostile Conservative government would block much progress before then while any new Labour government would need more than a month to conclude a treaty.
British Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government is opposed to many of the changes being floated at the IGC, notably anything that smacks of a loss of sovereignty.
At the summit, Major again criticised his colleagues for moving too quickly without thought for the consequences.
"Look before you leap is a much better watchword for the EU than leap before you look," he told reporters.

Major said he had told European Parliament President Klaus Haensch that he was offended by comments that Britain was out of step with Europe and had conducted blackmail during the "beef war" over mad cow disease earlier this year.

Three socialist leaders -- Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, Portugal's Antonio Guterres and the Netherlands' Wim Kok -- also angered Major last week by endorsing British opposition leader Tony Blair.
In other decisions, the summit decided to send Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring to the Middle East to offer the bloc's help in the peace process between Israelis and Palestinians.
It was in part a reflection of the frustration of the bloc, which is the main financer of peace in the region, to being left out of U.S.-led peace moves.
The leaders of Portugal, Spain and Italy, meanwhile, all said they were committed to joining the European Union's planned single currency from the start.
